articles.title_orig: Trump Backs Huang Comeback While Nvidia’s Board Pursues New CEO
articles.title_zh: Trump Backs Huang Comeback While Nvidia’s Board Pursues New CEO
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said he would be open to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returning to the company he resigned from last week amid the fallout from an extramarital relationship he had with an alleged Chinese spy.
"I think he learned a big lesson," Trump said of Huang when asked by reporters on Monday whether he wants to see the company co-founder reinstated as CEO.
Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House before departing for a trip to Asia, downplayed national security concerns stemming from the affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based technology company that U.S. officials suspect of having funneled Nvidia's advanced chips to China.
"It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns. Trump is due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.
The president told reporters he is not planning to replace Howard Lutnick as commerce secretary after questions arose about the Cabinet member's handling of export controls involving Nvidia's advanced chips.
Republican and Democratic members of Congress have raised concerns about the national security implications of the episode after it was revealed that Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in the 1990s, had an extramarital affair with Chinese businesswoman and alleged spy Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading global supplier of advanced artificial intelligence chips.
Critics argue the affair could jeopardize the U.S.' global dominance in AI and that it raises questions about influence exerted by Nvidia's Huang on regulators and lawmakers as he opposed export controls that limited the sale of the company's chips to Chinese firms.
The New York Times reported Tuesday that the U.S. believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and that Secretary of State Marco Rubio alerted Trump to the situation aboard Air Force One in May before Jensen Huang joined the president on a flight to China.
The Washington Post reported Friday that Rubio had issued a memo to Trump warning the president about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
But Trump on Monday said "I haven't heard that" when asked about Rubio's warning.
"I don't know that she is a spy. Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Trump said, of Alice Huang. "I don't know that she was a spy at all."
Trump also attempted to defuse tension bubbling within his Cabinet between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Lutnick.
Axios reported last week that Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China,  prompting a Situation Room confrontation between the men. Both are traveling with Trump on Monday to Asia, as is Rubio.
And Bessent, in an appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday, seemed to express frustration at Lutnick for not putting Megaspeed, Alice Huang's former company, on a Commerce Department list of companies that pose national security concerns.
The departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the 'entity list' for months," Bessent said.
Trump acknowledged on Monday that Lutnick might have delayed putting Megaspeed on the list but defended his rationale as essential for diplomacy.
"He was doing that because you could have — if you didn't delay it, If you didn't do something — you could have a blow-up with China," Trump said. "We're having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I'll make a decision. But I understand very well both sides."
Trump, who previously had said he did not plan to raise the Jensen Huang issue with Xi when they meet this week, said he may do so. He also said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.
As Trump downplays concerns about fallout from the affair and advanced chips finding their way to China, Capitol Hill leaders are taking a different approach .
A spokesperson for House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., told CNBC "negotiations are still going" about Jensen Huang testifying before a trio of House committees.
Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford, R-Ark., had given Huang a deadline of 8 p.m. ET Friday to respond to their request to appear before the committees. Mast has said he would subpoena the former CEO if he doesn't accept the invitation voluntarily.

articles.title_orig: The Death of ‘Keep 1.5 Alive’
articles.title_zh: The Death of ‘Keep 1.5 Alive’
articles.content_orig:
There was a reason, 11 years ago in Paris, that world leaders set themselves a target to keep the global rise in temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius compared with preindustrial levels. Beyond that, climate scientists say, warming will dangerously change our way of life.
We got a taste of it this year, as temperatures rose above the threshold for several months. Heat waves. Wildfires. Flash floods. And with a super El Niño year unfolding, next year might be worse. As one climate expert put it to me: This El Niño will effectively offer a time machine to the 2030s, showing what will happen if we don’t radically cut carbon emissions.
My colleague David Gelles, host of the Climate Forward newsletter, has been following the much diminished U.N. climate talks in Turkey. Today he writes about the death of 1.5 degrees and what that means for the planet.
It was the climate movement’s unifying slogan for the past decade: “Keep 1.5 Alive.”
The tagline referred to the central ambition of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

articles.title_orig: Trump Will Miss Most of the ASEAN Summit
articles.title_zh: Trump Will Miss Most of the ASEAN Summit
articles.content_orig:
For the second year in a row, President Trump is attending the annual gathering of Southeast Asian leaders, a show of alliance to a region that the United States sees as a strategic and maritime counterweight to China.
But Mr. Trump will reach the gathering, held this year in Manila, only on Tuesday, just as the summit wraps up, and he is not expected to make any significant policies or diplomacy moves.
Mixed signals like this — to say nothing of Mr. Trump’s punishing tariffs — are adding to a widespread belief within ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, that the United States is not a reliable partner. That leaves the bloc balancing between Washington and Beijing, with which many of its members have deep trade partnerships.
“They’ve learned that the United States is not reliable, so a lot of the hedging has been away from the United States,” said Ted Osius, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam.
The Philippines, America’s oldest security ally in Asia, provides a window into this balancing act.
After taking office three years ago, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. reversed his predecessor’s tilt toward China and pivoted back toward the United States. That stance contributed to many tense encounters between Filipino and Chinese vessels in the South China Sea, where Manila and Beijing have competing territorial claims.

articles.title_orig: Prime Minister Carney advances Canada’s strategic partnership with China across trade, commerce, and culture
articles.title_zh: Prime Minister Carney advances Canada’s strategic partnership with China across trade, commerce, and culture
articles.content_orig:
Over the past year and a half, Canada’s government has recalibrated our relationship with China – strategically, pragmatically, and decisively. Last January, the Prime Minister, Mark Carney, and the President of the People’s Republic of China, Xi Jinping, launched a new Canada-China strategic partnership to stabilise trade, build out clean energy industries, and better connect our peoples. Under the partnership, Canada and China have strengthened economic and financial cooperation, expanded cultural exchanges, and reduced tariffs on Canadian exports of canola seed and meal, peas, crab, and lobster. To date, Canada has restored market access for more than 90% of trade previously subject to tariff action – nearly $7.5 billion worth of Canadian exports.
To build on that success, Prime Minister Carney today met with President Xi in Shenzhen, China. The leaders agreed on new measures that will further expand trade between their two countries.
Canada and China are announcing:
To create more opportunities for investment, education, and exchanges between our countries, Prime Minister Carney announced:
The expanded partnership between Canada and China is also at play in the private sector. During the visit, Prime Minister Carney and President Xi welcomed the following agreements and investments from businesses:
The leaders also discussed the positive outcomes of recent dialogues between Canada and China to increase border and customs cooperation against narcotics threats, and to enhance collaboration on oil and gas, renewable energy, and nuclear with key industry leaders from the energy sector.
As the world’s second-largest economy and a country of more than 1.4 billion people, China plays a central role in Canada’s engagement in the Indo-Pacific. Across Canada, hundreds of thousands of jobs are supported by trade with China – from farmers in the Prairies to manufacturers in Ontario and Québec and fish harvesters in Atlantic Canada and British Columbia. Our trade with China generates over $30 billion in revenues and adds $6.9 billion to Canada’s GDP. By expanding Canada’s access to one of the world’s largest markets, we are opening new avenues for commercial, scientific, and cultural collaboration, and strengthening the ties between our peoples.
In Shenzhen, Prime Minister Carney will represent Canada at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders’ Meeting to further deepen our partnerships across the region.
“Canada and China have recalibrated our relationship to the benefit of citizens in both countries. We have unlocked billions in new export orders for Canadian farmers, ranchers, and fish harvesters – for workers and businesses across the country. We’re making it easier to travel, study, and do business between our nations to create more opportunity and prosperity for all. Canada is building our strength at home and diversifying our relationships abroad so that we have the freedom to live our lives as we choose.”
The Rt. Hon. Mark Carney, Prime Minister of Canada

articles.title_orig: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
articles.title_zh: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
US president Donald Trump heads to Asia this week to take part in back-to-back summits on economic cooperation, world conflicts, and nuclear weapons.
Much of the world’s focus will be on the historic, first-ever trilateral meeting between Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday.
However, hours before leaving the White House for the Philippines, Trump managed to raise the stakes even further while suggesting North Korean leader could also join them.
“(Xi) was here a month ago, and we're also going to meet with (Russian) President Putin, and we may meet with Kim Jong Un also,” Trump said.
“So that'll be good. We have a chance to accomplish a lot.,” while stressing the decision on Kim’s attendance was up to Beijing.
Despite the strategic importance of the issues on the agenda during the trip, it could still be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal.
CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign last week after it emerged he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The ousted tech boss has close ties to the US president, even accompanying him on Air Force One during his last trip to China in May.
However Trump is not expected to directly raise the spy allegations with Xi, one senior US administration told Reuters on condition of anonymity.
The US president is due tol land in Manila on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit, before flying to Shenzhen in southern China late on Wednesday for the two-day Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum, at the end of which the first-ever three-way discussion between Xi, Trump, and ‌Putin will take place.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” said a White House spokesperson.
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February. It is the first time since the early 1970s that there is no legally binding limits on US and Russian nuclear forces without another agreement being under negotiation.
Russia and the US possess the largest nuclear arsenal in the world, followed by China.
The United Nations has long urged for nuclear disarmament, warning that rising geopolitical tensions have fuelled nuclear risks around the world.
“If there is a denuclearisation program, we are ready to be fully engaged in that and contribute to make it a success,” UN ​Secretary-General Antonio ‌Guterres said on Monday in Manila, where he is attending the Asean summit.
The denuclearisation talks will also spotlight the war in Iran, with Tehran being a strategic partner of both China and Russia.
Leaders at Asean are likely to renew calls for peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including in the South China Sea and in Myanmar. They are expected to push for efforts to protect their economies and citizens from the continuing fallout from global conflicts, such as the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf.
The White House has said that Trump plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand while in Manila, while US officials will also meet on the sidelines with the so-called Quad, or Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, which consists of Australia, India, Japan and the US.
Trump will be looking for an overseas success on the trip, following the disastrous midterm results that saw his Republican party lose control of Congress.
“The president will undoubtedly be seeking to use this trip to reassert leadership, authority, demonstrate his statesmanship capabilities and essentially show off on the international stage,” Kurt Tong, a former US ambassador for Apec, told Bloomberg.
The US president will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday.
But expectations for progress at the talks in China are not high. No agreement is expected afterward, a senior US official said, according to AP and Reuters.
“In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi,” US-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling told PBS News .
“With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises,” he said.
Other critical issues at these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition.

articles.title_orig: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
articles.title_zh: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
articles.content_orig:
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko at the site of a missile strike in October
Two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital have reportedly been struck in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The missiles hit Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges spanning the Dnipro River, Klitschko said, adding that water and power supplies had been disrupted.
Meanwhile, Ukraine struck the landmark Kerch Bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea killing two people, the region's Moscow-installed governor said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky had earlier warned that Moscow might launch further strikes on the country on Monday night, after Ukrainian, US and European officials held further talks aimed at ending the years-long conflict.
Those online talks, attended by US envoy Jared Kushner and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, came after Russia said it recorded the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems".
"Some areas are experiencing disruptions to water and heating supplies", he added.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services have been damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Residents of Kyiv typically shelter in the city's underground stations during air raids.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv. An estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Several of the capital's major bridges were also targeted by Russian drone strikes in October .
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.
Separately, the Ukrainian military struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea for a second consecutive day , the region's Moscow-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov said on Telegram.
Traffic across the bridge had been suspended, he added.
The landmark bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014.
Russian President Vladimir Putin inaugurated the bridge to great fanfare in 2018. The severity of the latest strike on Kerch Bridge is still unclear, though it is protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.
Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.
The latest round of tit-for-tat strikes came after US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks on ways to facilitate "direct engagement" between Russia and Europe to end the war.
Following Monday's meeting, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, said the US was committed to providing Ukraine with a "strong, credible security guarantees", as well as a path towards EU membership.
He added that Nato "will remain a critical pillar of European security", and that preparations are underway for a further multilateral meeting "in the near future".
In an address on Monday evening, Zelensky said that the meeting was "difficult", adding that more needed to be done to support Ukraine's defence against Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Zelensky said that Europe was represented for the first time by the full delegation that will participate in negotiations with Moscow - including the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the EU and Nato.
The Ukrainian president has long called for European delegates to be included in any peace talks, which he argues is necessary because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
He also said that Moscow is receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials said that the final death toll from a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian village of Kamyshuvakha earlier this month had reached 72.
Four people are still considered missing after the bombing, which Ukrainian officials say is one of the deadliest individual attacks since the start of the war in 2022.
Footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, showed residents going to an underground shelter after the initial attack on 2 November. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
Ukrainian police said of those killed were police officers, "staff of the gymnasium, utility workers and medical personnel".
Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title_orig: Major banking outage linked to Chase, impacted Wells Fargo and BofA
articles.title_zh: Major banking outage linked to Chase, impacted Wells Fargo and BofA
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of customers across the United States reported problems accessing banking services and making payments after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted transactions involving other banks.
The problems on Monday affected customers at several major financial institutions, including Wells Fargo and Bank of America, while some users also reported delays with Zelle payments.
So, what caused the US bank outages, which banks were affected, and have services returned to normal?
Thousands of US customers reported problems accessing online banking services after JPMorgan Chase said a software issue caused knock-on effects for transactions involving other banks.
The disruption extended to customers of at least five other banks, who reported issues accessing services and completing transactions.
According to the French news agency AFP, reports on outage-tracking Downdetector peaked at around 2pm Eastern Standard Time (19:00 GMT) before declining later in the day.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system – it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesperson for the bank.
Customers of several major US banks reported problems on Monday.
These included JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, US Bank, Truist and Capital One.
However, not all the banks reported problems with their own systems.
Chase confirmed experiencing technical problems, while US Bank said its own systems were not directly affected. Capital One and Truist also said their services were operating normally.
JPMorgan Chase said that a software bug in its internal hardware systems had slowed transaction processing and may have delayed transactions involving other banks.
Some customers said they were not able to access accounts and funds, although Chase said customers continued to have access.
The bank stressed that the disruption was not systemic and that other banks may have experienced delays when processing transactions involving Chase.
Chase is the consumer banking division of JPMorgan Chase, which holds the most assets of any US bank. It handles payments involving other financial institutions, meaning a technical problem at Chase can also delay transactions for customers at other banks, even if those banks’ systems are operating normally.
“This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” Evangelisti added.
Zelle is the peer-to-peer third-party payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed.
It is owned by Early Warning Services, an Arizona-based company that is itself owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.
In the US, some customers also reported problems sending and receiving payments through Zelle.
However, Zelle said its network was operating normally.
The company said that customers access Zelle through participating banks and credit unions so technical problems at those institutions can affect the ability to make a payment even if Zelle’s own systems are fully operational.
US Bank said its systems were not directly affected but warned that customers sending or receiving Zelle payments involving other financial institutions could experience delays.
JPMorgan Chase said that transactions were processing normally again following the disruption.
A Chase spokesperson said that shortly after close of business on Monday, at approximately 6:30pm (23:30 GMT), transactions were posting normally, according to NBC News.
However, the restoration of Chase’s transaction processing does not necessarily mean every delayed payment has been completed.
There is no confirmed connection between Monday’s outages and the recent Microsoft outage and disruptions impacting the US government’s transport agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
The banking problems followed two major incidents in the US last week.
On Thursday, Microsoft experienced a widespread outage that disrupted services including Outlook. A day later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop following a technical failure affecting air traffic control communications.
The incidents had different reported causes. JPMorgan Chase said its disruption was due to a software bug, while the FAA disruption involved malfunctioning equipment.
However, Jody Westby, CEO of cybersecurity advisory firm Global Cyber Risk, told Al Jazeera that the series of incidents raised questions about the reliability and security of critical infrastructure.
“I think it’s very concerning that everyone’s just jumping to the conclusion it’s a technical issue, it’s a software bug, it was old equipment,” she said.
“I don’t think that any of that is a complete explanation the public deserves.”
Westby said she believed more detailed investigations were needed.
“My concern is that we are not diligently looking into these incidents and analysing them, and even with a global working group to make sure that we can determine whether there are any correlations.”

articles.title_orig: Trump administration's $50B air traffic demand hits GOP turbulence in the Senate
articles.title_zh: Trump administration's $50B air traffic demand hits GOP turbulence in the Senate
articles.content_orig:
The air traffic control tower at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in Los Angeles, California, on Nov. 14, 2026.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday blamed the previous day’s nationwide ground stop on the replacement of copper wires at a “remote” Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) facility. Installing new fiber optic lines led to critical communication breakdowns, he said.
About 7,500 flights were delayed and over 9,000 were canceled on Friday, according to FlightAware . Some 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. Eastern, shortly after the ground stop began.
The incident raised questions about what might have led to the historic event—only the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11—and what authorities were doing to prevent it from happening again.
“What we’re working to determine is whether we had incompetence,” Duffy said Saturday, which saw nearly 6,000 additional flights canceled. "Or did they install a faulty router?"
As investigators continued working to pinpoint the source of the problem, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters in Washington, D.C., that disrupted flight schedules were expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday and promised that the “worst is behind us.”
While that may be true for this specific outage, Duffy warned Friday that what happened was not an isolated incident and said that outages would likely continue to occur until antiquated communications equipment across the FAA’s air traffic control network was brought up to date.
“It was the old legacy equipment. It failed,” Duffy said. “And listen, it’s going to continue to fail.”
The Transportation Secretary went on to call for Congress to provide $50 billion before the end of the year to upgrade air traffic control and airport infrastructure, increasing the administration’s recent $30.1 billion request, which included $10.1 billion specifically for air traffic control modernization.
President Donald Trump addressed the outage for the first time on Sunday, urging Congress to approve additional funding in a post on Truth Social . “If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” he said.
There is reason to believe, however, that financial support alone will not solve the problems currently faced by the FAA. Those include shortages in fully certified air traffic controllers, weaknesses in planning and coordinating necessary modernization work, and vulnerabilities to cybersecurity threats.
TIME has reached out to Duffy’s office for comment.
Modernizing the FAA’s air traffic control system has been a goal of the industry for years, says Edward Booth, an aviation attorney and pilot based in Jacksonville, and billions of dollars have already been sunk into the process.
“There has been a very methodical four-part, four-stage plan to upgrade that,” Booth tells TIME, referencing NextGen , a multibillion-dollar FAA modernization initiative dating to 2003. It has included shifting toward satellite-based aircraft tracking, digital communications, and more efficient flight routes.
Booth says a major focus of those earlier modernization efforts was making more efficient use of airspace.
“They have tried to squeeze more airplanes into limited space, make better use of the limited runways available in the system, and they started with completely changing the way airplanes are tracked in the world. It's a world standard now,” he says, pointing to how NextGen has already made strides in air travel.
The agency’s newer overhaul builds on earlier modernization work and includes replacing aging communications equipment, radar, and other infrastructure, with its first phase targeted for completion by the end of 2028.
“It's a very highly technical, robust system,” Booth says of the National Airspace System (NAS), “but it seems the weak spot was discovered yesterday afternoon.”
For more than two decades, the FAA has been working to modernize the NAS while fighting an uphill battle against aging infrastructure. The average U.S. air traffic control tower was 40 years old, and most radar systems were approaching that age, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Chairman Sam Graves wrote in a May 2025 op-ed .
Congress had already ordered an independent review of the FAA’s aging technology: The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required an audit of legacy systems deployed before 2000—including their vulnerability to single-point failures—and a plan to accelerate replacement or improvement of those found to pose risks. In a written response to Congress , the FAA said that nonprofit research organization MITRE completed the audit in August 2025. The response said the findings would guide modernization efforts, but did not disclose the specific findings or resulting actions.
In July 2025, Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA to upgrade its “radar, software, hardware, and telecommunications” at more than 4,600 sites through December 2028.
As of Nov. 5, the FAA said it has “replaced 69% of copper wires, installed Surface Awareness Initiative (SAI) systems at 143 towers, transitioned 26 towers to electronic flight strips [and] installed 226 IP Voice Switches.”
The updates were noted within an announcement saying the FAA was beginning to phase out the floppy disks used in air traffic control. It said that it had launched a replacement system that would include a digital display board with data about disruptions, weather conditions, and advisories. The announcement identified five initial facilities and set a goal of installing the system at 435 sites by the end of 2028.
Duffy called these efforts “the latest signal that America’s brand new air traffic control system is coming at lightning speed.”
The FAA then announced Nov. 10 that it was expanding its AI-powered scheduling and flight-planning tool—known as SMART (Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories)—to airspace managed by all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers nationwide. SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million contract that also covers the agency’s Flow Management Data and Services program.
Duffy said at Friday’s press conference that SMART had nothing to do with the disruption.
Describing Friday's outage, Duffy said a router being replaced as workers switched from copper wiring to fiber-optic connections began flooding other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting communications and some radar feeds. Systems came back online after officials isolated the work at the remote location, he said.
For Booth, the spread of that disruption underscores the need for safeguards that can contain a problem in one part of the FAA’s communications network before it affects the wider system.
“They need a system that is not prone to single-point failures,” he says.
Booth pointed out that legacy systems—often relying on analog lines, decades-old routers, and interconnected regional hubs—lack the fault-tolerant design needed to prevent a local or routine maintenance glitch from cascading nationwide.
“The public probably would be shocked to learn that the way pilots communicate with air traffic control is tantamount to an old-fashioned telephone line,” he says. “You've got 10, sometimes 15 airplanes competing to talk to a single controller-specified frequency.”
Kumar Sokka, the CEO of Acre Security, says a key consideration when upgrading complex systems is whether individual components can fail without disrupting the entire network.
“Can you remove a single point of failure? Are these systems distributed in a way where it's siloed in certain structures where if something fails, not everything fails, right?” asks Sokka.
He says that many industries come up against issues of balancing the high upfront expense of upgrading legacy systems against the severe financial and operational risks of future outages.

articles.title_orig: Study estimates magnitude of US data center pollution as climate talks unveil clean AI pledge
articles.title_zh: Study estimates magnitude of US data center pollution as climate talks unveil clean AI pledge
articles.content_orig:
An aerial shows a 49.5 megawatt three-level data center under construction on Oct. 29, 2026 in Vernon, California.
America’s hyperscale data centers together use as much electricity as some entire U.S. states and produce millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide over the course of a year, according to a new study published Monday in Nature Sustainability .
The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models , has exploded in recent years. Between 2019 and 2024, the number of data centers around the world doubled from a little over 500 to over 1,100, with more than half located in the United States. That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers .
American voters rallied against data center development in the midterm elections this November, with many citing economic and environmental concerns. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development. Yet few studies have quantified just how much electricity each hyperscale data center uses, and what fuels generate the electricity, the researchers say.
“Even though there were a lot of [public and scientific] statements about the environmental impact of data centers, when we started this research, we realized that there was basically very little, if none, peer-reviewed data,” says Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative and senior author of the paper.
The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of hyperscale data centers since the rise of AI. The researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 hyperscale data centers across the U.S., and then estimated the annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used data from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to calculate their emissions.
They found that, together, the data centers used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity—with the upper estimate equivalent to what some states, like Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. In the lower scenario, the facilities still consumed approximately the annual electricity sold to customers in Wisconsin, roughly 70 TWh, or Minnesota, around 65 TWh.
More than half of the electricity powering the data centers comes from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The facilities studied produced a combined estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide—roughly the annual emissions of Denmark.
Half of the electricity use of all the data centers studied was concentrated in just four states: Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa, the report found. Virginia has long been known as “data center alley” due to its high number of data centers, but size and power capacity can also impact electricity consumption. The researchers identified 26 hyperscale facilities in Iowa, combined electricity consumption for which was approximately 7.2 TWh, with the average facility having substantially higher estimated electricity demand than the average facility in Virginia, where 142 hyperscale facilities account for approximately 21.4 TWh of annual electricity consumption.
However, the emissions impacts were not always the same. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio have the most emissions attributable to hyperscale data centers, while Oregon, which is home to more hyperscale data centers than Iowa and Ohio, has significantly fewer emissions due to a cleaner energy grid.
“For the same amount of electricity consumed, the regional electricity mix associated with data centers in Wyoming produces approximately seven times more carbon dioxide than in Oregon,” says Gianluca Guidi, Harvard data scientist and the study’s lead author. “So these environmental impacts are not necessarily inevitable. Geography matters.”
Without clean energy alternatives, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than most countries by 2035, according to a report from BloombergNEF.
The electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely even higher than the research shows. The team did not have enough data to assess every single hyperscale data center in the U.S. at the time, and more data centers have emerged since their study concluded in April 2025.
The researchers hope to continue to quantify the environmental impacts of hyperscale data centers to better understand their impact on air pollution, water, and health, adding that, as AI continues to scale, its infrastructure growth must be done sustainably.
“We tend to imagine AI as something that is almost immaterial, but in the end, the infrastructure power is profoundly physical,” says Guidi. “Behind every algorithm, there are enormous buildings, power plants, water resources, and ultimately also communities that live with the consequences.”

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang conducts an interview on Oct. 14. Photo: Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Jensen Huang's self-destruction has left a trail of collateral damage that threatens to ensnare the board of Nvidia and the AI boom itself .
Why it matters: Huang was a singular leader in the global economy, capable of exciting or calming markets with a single sentence and viewed as a virtually indestructible force behind Nvidia's rise.
The big picture: His sudden exit after reports of multiple affairs — one with a suspected Chinese spy and the other with a direct report — has wiped out more than $600 billion in value from Nvidia's market cap.
Zoom in: With the uncertainty over Huang's tenure at Nvidia now resolved, the attention will quickly pivot to a slew of unanswered questions, including:
What will the investigations uncover?
Critics say the Nvidia board wasn't fulfilling its duty to provide proper oversight of Huang — particularly if it had any reason to be aware of his reported affairs before they become public.
Who takes the permanent role as CEO?
Threat level: Could this be the catalyst that pops the AI bubble?
Next week becomes a "critical" moment with Tuesday's Nvidia earnings report and Thursday's likely Anthropic IPO, Shulman says.
The other side: Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at consultancy West Monroe, argued that Huang's departure won't change the demand for chips:
Follow the money: Will Huang's exit fundamentally reshape the long-term competitive landscape of the chip industry?
What's the floor for Nvidia's stock?
The intrigue: Will someone take a risk on hiring Huang?
The bottom line: The fallout is just beginning.

articles.title_orig: Asia shares slide on tech weakness ahead of Nvidia earnings
articles.title_zh: Asia shares slide on tech weakness ahead of Nvidia earnings
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks dropped as investors braced for a momentous week for the artificial intelligence trade, with the Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) IPO and Nvidia ( NVDA ) first post-Jensen Huang earnings day on deck.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 1.4%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) declined by roughly 1.9%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 2.5% after stocks made gains last week despite increased volatility.
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 4% during Monday trading as investors mulled what comes next for the chip giant in the wake of its board ousting former CEO Jensen Huang. The board is not considering bringing back Huang, according to a Monday CNBC report. An earlier Financial Times report said Huang and his Silicon Valley allies are discussing a campaign to reinstate him , an idea that President Trump also publicly backed.
On Tuesday, Nvidia will report third quarter results — a consequential earnings report in any typical quarter, but especially significant given Huang's scandal and departure.
That is expected to be followed by Anthropic's IPO on Thursday , which could set the record for the largest public debut of all time and set the tone for OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) eventual IPO. Anthropic is targeting a valuation of around $1.4 trillion.
Oil prices ( CL=F ) dipped , with Brent crude ( BZ=F ) declining to $92 per barrel, as shipments through the Strait of Hormuz continue to recover despite the US ramping up its military presence in the Middle East, as a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the region.
United Airlines ( UAL ) stock fell 3% after the company said it is experiencing a "widespread system outage."
Travelers reported being stuck on flights on the tarmac while they waited for the issue to be resolved.
The outage comes just days after the FAA issued a rare ground stop to all flights due to a "temporary telecommunications outage." On Monday, banking apps and payment services also experienced disruption due to a software bug. Microsoft Outlook also faced a disruption last week.
US stocks sank as Nvidia ( NVDA ) led the semiconductor sector lower following tightened restrictions on advanced chips abroad.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) dropped 1.4%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) declined by more than 1.9%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) sank roughly 2.5%.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
Nvidia shares fell roughly 4% after reports said the AI chip giant's board was not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO. Weekend speculation that Silicon Valley executives were pushing for Huang's return was dampened, despite President Trump's public support for the move.
Meanwhile, tighter US restrictions aimed at preventing circumvention of controls on semiconductor access to China weighed on the broader chip sector.
Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports:
Something pretty remarkable is happening in Silicon Valley right now. One shouldn't be surprised, considering the profit motives of many invested in the AI ecosystem and that what Nvidia ( NVDA ) does lies at the center of it all.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned as the company's CEO under a cloud of controversy he created, and suddenly some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley are organizing a campaign to bring him back.
Tesla ( TSLA ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) CEO Elon Musk has signed on to the "Bring Jensen Back" petition. Other prominent executives have joined, including Uber ( UBER ) founder Travis Kalanick — who left Uber unceremoniously after his own string of highly publicized missteps.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) extended declines to session lows on Monday, sinking 4% and dragging the rest of the "Magnificent Seven" group with it.
A snapshot of Yahoo Finance's AlphaSpace data shows t he AI chip giant down 4% while Alphabet ( GOOGL ) shares are down more than 3%. Amazon ( AMZN ) stock is also 3% lower, followed by Meta (META) and Tesla ( TSLA ).
The tech sector retreated, with semiconductor stocks leading the decline after the US tightened restrictions on overseas access to advanced semiconductors.
Reports of bank app outages are causing bank stocks to fall in midday trading. Shares of Bank of America ( BAC ), Citigroup ( C ), Wells Fargo ( WFC ), and JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) fell by around 2%.
Downdetector.com, which tracks online outages, showed customers' reports of issues spiked across a number of sites, including Chase, US Bank, Truist, and Zelle, which is owned by a privately held company, owned by Bank of America, Truist, Capital Ones, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, US Bank, and Wells Fargo.
"Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible," a JPMorgan spokesperson told Yahoo Finance.
Bank of America ( BAC ) CEO Brian Moynihan gave investors another reason to pay close attention to Anthropic's blockbuster IPO this week.
The Claude maker's massive stock market debut is pushing some smaller companies to delay their own listings until 2027, Moynihan said Monday on Bloomberg TV.
Moynihan said his investment bankers told him over the weekend that companies in more traditional industries, including biotechnology, are postponing offerings to give investors time to digest Anthropic's listing.
"It's just trying to let the market settle in after this major transaction," he added.
Bank of America is estimated to earn around $9 million in underwriting fees from the listing, according to analysis from Evercore ISI.
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board of directors is reportedly not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO of the AI chip giant.
According to a CNBC report citing a person familiar with the matter, the board is focused on a national security investigation into Huang and is not considering bringing him back.
Nvidia stock fell to session lows after the report.
Huang resigned last Thursday after reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected of spying for China.
President Trump on Monday weighed in on the issue, casting doubt on whether the woman was a spy and saying that Huang did not put national security at risk. Trump also supported bringing Huang back to the company.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
Intel ( INTC ) stock fell more than 6% Monday morning as the market reacted to news that the company is facing a class action lawsuit from investors, Yahoo Finance's Paige Oamek reports:
In the lawsuit filed on Friday , Intel shareholders claim the technology company misled investors about the impact of a slowdown in PC sales on its revenue. The complaint also claims Intel hid that supply limits blocked the company from meeting data center demand.
When those realities came to light in Intel's third quarter earnings report last month, shares dropped 28.6% the next day, losing around $140 billion of market value in the company's largest single-day decline in more than 50 years.
Vanda Research is telling clients that Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) highly anticipated IPO later this week could attract record buying from everyday investors. But some of that demand may come at the expense of other artificial intelligence stocks.
Vanda Research cautioned clients on Monday that the AI startup's stock market debut could draw money away from tech giants and other data center infrastructure companies that investors have used to gain exposure to the AI boom.
Until now, investors seeking exposure to leading AI developers have largely had to invest indirectly through publicly traded companies backing them or supplying their infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: White House "tiger team" formed to prevent another nationwide ground stop
articles.title_zh: White House "tiger team" formed to prevent another nationwide ground stop
articles.content_orig:
Days after a debilitating nationwide ground stop, the Trump administration’s push for emergency funding for the nation’s aging air traffic control system is running into resistance from top Republicans on Capitol Hill.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy issued an urgent demand this weekend for as much as $50 billion after halted flights left over a million passengers stranded on Friday.
But key Republicans – including Senate Majority Leader John Thune – are demanding more information about that request, including what the administration had done with the last sizable tranche of funding meant to upgrade those air systems. And few lawmakers believe the GOP-led Congress will be able to deliver that money in the final weeks of their power, before the Democratic takeover begins in January.
“I think it’s highly unlikely that Congress is just going to write a check for $50 billion just because he says so,” GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas said of Duffy’s request.
He added that any push to spend that kind of money – a sum that rivals the annual appropriations for many government departments – would need far more time to win approval from Congress.
“When you do things really fast around here, you make mistakes. And that’s why the whole system is designed to move methodically and deliberatively,” Cornyn warned.
Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to update air traffic control systems as part of President Donald Trump’s massive spending and policy bill – which many lawmakers, including Thune, have argued has not yet been fully spent.
“About $8 billion of that [is] still sitting around,” Thune said on Monday of the initial $12.5 billion tranche. “I mean there’s some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is,” he added, arguing Congress has “attempted to do what we can to ensure that the concerns they have about modernization” are answered.
Others in GOP leadership are privately baffled — or even frustrated — by Duffy’s attempt to blame Congress for a funding shortfall, despite Republicans doling out billions last year, according to multiple sources. Republicans aren’t ruling out more money for air traffic modernization — a decades-long priority for both parties. But they’re making clear that they won’t simply rubber stamp $50 billion – or any amount – without clarity from the White House about where the money has gone so far.
“What I think a lot of people don’t realize is that the FAA has not spent the money that we previously appropriated — and that part of that money was designated to beautify airports. That should not be the priority. We do have a serious problem with our air traffic control system,” said GOP Sen. Susan Collins, a top Senate appropriator who said she was briefed over the weekend by the FAA administrator.
But, of the request for more funding, she said: “I don’t see the justification yet for that much.”
Another reason for the hesitation in Congress: Lawmakers are not entirely clear on what happened to ground flights on Friday. Some key lawmakers will briefed behind closed doors on Tuesday. And Duffy will meet with Senate Republicans over lunch on Capitol Hill, according to a source familiar.
“Well, we gave them $12.5 billion,” Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, a member of GOP leadership, said when asked about Duffy’s finger-pointing at Congress amid fallout over the decision to ground flights.
Duffy has said though that his agency does not have the funding it needs.
“I have no money in that $12.5 billion that I can use for a new architecture for telecom. I can’t build new software to manage our airplanes in the airspace because it dates back to the 1990s, but there’s no money for that. There’s no money for towers. Our towers are old,” Duffy said on CNN’s “State of the Union” with Dana Bash on Sunday.
According to a source familiar with the plans, DOT has “allocated” all of the $12.5 billion to certain projects. However, the money is not deemed “spent” until those specific projects are installed and operational. Several of the DOT’s plans are underway, the source said. Duffy has publicly stated the $12.5 billion will be spent by the end of December 2028.
According to a fact sheet from the department, “Congress placed parameters on the funding outlining exactly how much of the total package could be spent on specific categories of work. The Department does not have the legal flexibility to move funds from one workstream to another,” the release states.
“As the Department has made clear for the last two years – separate funding is needed to cover separate work streams,” it states, citing efforts such as modernizing the digital architecture powering air traffic control and upgrading and replacing aviation infrastructure.
GOP Sen. Rand Paul repeatedly called for an accounting of where the $12.5 billion has gone. “I think a methodical look at what happened, what mistakes were made, where the money is being spent, before we just immediately throw more money at the problem,” he said.
GOP Sen. John Kennedy made clear he wants Duffy to explain why they need the money. “I want him to sit me down and explain to me what happened and the problem, like he’s talking to a moderately intelligent ninth grader.”
“Then I want him to explain how it’s going to be fixed, when it’s going to be fixed, who’s going to fix it, and how much it’s going to cost,” he said.
As of June, the agency had spent only $474.9 million of the $12.5 billion Congress had appropriated, according to data from a congressional source shared with CNN.
Congress appropriated $1.9 billion to specifically help build a new air traffic control center, for example, but none of that money had been spent by the agency as of June, the source told CNN.
The data shared with CNN shows that the FAA had $4.75 billion dedicated to telecommunications infrastructure and that only $309 million had been spent as of June.
At least one Republican said he has been rattled by a string of high-profile outages across the US – including that nationwide ground stop – and wants to probe whether any of the incidents are related.
“I want a deeper dive. I think we too quickly dismissed that there was no malicious acts,” Sen. Tim Sheehy, a former Navy SEAL and combat veteran, said on Monday. “We had Microsoft go down on Thursday, air traffic go down on Friday, banks go down today. We have very sophisticated digital adversaries. That sounds a little too much of a coincidence to me. So before we dismiss that, I want to see the details on that.”
GOP Sen. Rick Scott of Florida, another senator with some of the nation’s busiest airports in his state, was noncommittal on whether he’d approve the funding.
“I think we have to get all the facts before we do anything…seeing how they’re going to use it,” Scott said. “We have to have a budget and what the timeline is, who’s going to do it, all that.”
CNN’s Ellis Kim and Alexandra Skores contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Stock Market News, November 16, 2026: Nasdaq Slides 2.5% as Nvidia Drama Continues
articles.title_zh: Stock Market News, November 16, 2026: Nasdaq Slides 2.5% as Nvidia Drama Continues
articles.content_orig:
A major week for Wall Street started on a down note. US markets closed lower Monday, led by declines in technology stocks associated with the artificial intelligence boom.
The S&P 500 fell 1.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739 points, or 1.4%. Wall Street’s fear gauge, the VIX, surged 19%.
Shares of Nvidia ( NVDA ) dropped 4.1%, falling for the third consecutive day since Jensen Huang resigned. Nvidia shares are coming off their worst week in 19 months. Investors are gearing up for Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, expected Tuesday after the market close.
Shares of the semiconductor chip designer have had a rocky few weeks, with the Huang scandal accelerating declines. Nvidia shares are down roughly 35% since a record high on October 6, erasing about $2 trillion in market value.
On Monday, shares of Nvidia closed at $156.14, their lowest level since July 1, 2025. Nvidia shares have erased all of their gains over the past 16 months. Nvidia stock was hit by a raft of Wall Street analysts slashing their price targets last week. At Evercore ISI, analysts cut their price target to $186, down from a prior target of $465. At HSBC, analysts cut their target to $170, down from $365.
Shares of semiconductor chipmakers, Big Tech and other companies involved in the data center buildout fell Monday. Intel shares ( INTC ) fell 7.1%, while Alphabet shares ( GOOG ) fell 3.85%. CoreWeave shares ( CRWV ) sank 6.1%.
The Commerce Department on Monday also tightened export controls designed to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips. The much-anticipated Commerce rule puts new curbs on US exports to data centers that provide “significant volumes” of computing to companies based in countries subject to US arms embargoes, such as China, Iran and Russia.
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq each gained more than 2% last week. The declines on Monday ate away at those gains. Overall, the S&P and Nasdaq are down roughly 5% and 11%, respectively, since record highs on October 6. The Dow is down 5% since its peak on August 5.
Investors are also gearing up for Anthropic’s expected initial public offering later this week. The AI frontier lab is targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion , and its IPO is a pivotal moment for the tech boom that has become a driving force for the US stock market.
“How investors view Nvidia’s updates against the recent turmoil left in the wake of Jensen Huang’s departure and the market reaction to Anthropic becoming a public company may determine whether the AI trade can gain its footing or whether hiccups here cause further damage across the ecosystem,” Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, wrote in a Monday note.

articles.title_orig: ‘It’s a horrible idea’: Republicans shut down talk of Jensen Huang’s return
articles.title_zh: ‘It’s a horrible idea’: Republicans shut down talk of Jensen Huang’s return
articles.content_orig:
Bill Ackman said there could be a case for reinstating Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO — that is, only if Huang is cleared of any wrongdoing related to putting his company's national security obligations at risk.
At a conference hosted by Semafor on Monday, the billionaire activist investor was asked what strategy he would use to pressure the board into reinstating Huang.
Huang resigned from his role on Thursday following the disclosure of extramarital affairs and concerns that he may have been a target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
Ackman said that if Huang's relationships were determined to be a "personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy," there could be a "powerful case" for putting Huang back in the CEO seat, though the investor said it would be "unlikely" for him to be involved in such an effort.
"You just present the facts, and you call a special meeting," he said, adding that an activist investor could also partner with Huang, who owns more than 3% of the company.
Said special meeting would be a shareholder vote on reinstating Huang. The now-former CEO's involvement would not only help the company meet the threshold for calling one — which requires at least 15% of the voting power — but also send a public message that the founder wants to return.
"You call a special meeting, the writing will be on the wall very quickly, I would expect, at which point you don't even have to go the meeting," Ackman said. "Just put him back in, make some changes to the board, and push forward."
A spokesperson for Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.
Ackman, who has defended Huang since the Nvidia founder's affairs were publicized, said the situation is an "interesting activist setup," given that Huang is a heralded founder who would have plenty of shareholder support .

articles.title_orig: The Important Gmail Security Settings You Should Be Using
articles.title_zh: The Important Gmail Security Settings You Should Be Using
articles.content_orig:
Having your Google account compromised can be a huge deal.
Gmail is no longer just an email service. Plenty of websites and apps let you log in with your Google account, and many people use that one login for almost everything they do online. It makes signing in a lot easier. It also means that whoever holds the keys to your account holds a lot more than just your private emails.
Google is very aware of that, which is why it offers a variety of security and privacy settings to keep your account safe and keep third parties out of it. These are some of the most important ones you should be using.
Start with Security Checkup ; it's a page in your Google Account that gives you personalized recommendations, like adding a recovery phone number and email. Those might sound like very basic steps, but they matter more than you might think: Google uses them to alert you to suspicious activity and to help you get back in if someone locks you out. From google.com, click your profile icon in the upper right, then click Manage your Google Account . Click Security & sign-in . At the top of the page, you'll see an icon. A green shield means nothing needs your attention right now. A blue, yellow or red exclamation mark means there's something to fix.
The single biggest fix is two-step verification, also known as two-factor authentication. With it on, a stolen password isn't enough, because signing in also takes something you physically have on you, like your phone or your own computer. To switch it on, go to Security & sign-in , find the How you sign in to Google section, select Turn on 2-Step Verification and follow the prompts.
Then there are passkeys, which let you sign in with your fingerprint, face scan or screen lock instead of a password. A passkey can't be shared, copied or written down, so it holds up against phishing. To create one, go to your account's passkey page and select Create a passkey . Only do it on devices you own; once a passkey exists, anyone who can unlock that device can get into your account.
Locking the front door doesn't help if someone already has a key, so check who and what is connected. Go to myaccount.google.com , open Security & sign-in and scroll down to the linked apps section, then select See all linked apps . You'll see the apps and sites you use Sign in with Google for, plus anything that has been given access to your account data. Anything you don't recognize or no longer use can go: select Remove access , then Confirm .
Next, look at Gmail itself. An attacker who gets in often changes a few quiet settings so they can keep reading your mail later. Open Gmail on your computer, click the gear icon in the top right and select See all settings . Then check for anything unfamiliar under automatic forwarding, filters, labels, scheduled emails, your vacation responder, and IMAP or POP access. Mail delegation, which lets someone else read, send and delete email in your account, has its own spot: go to the Accounts and Import tab and look under Grant access to your account . If a name is there that you didn't add, click Delete next to it. You can't manage delegates from the Gmail app, only on the desktop site. Automatic forwarding is the nasty one. It sends a copy of every new message, except spam, to another address, and you'd never notice. If you find a forwarding rule you didn't set up, change your password right away and turn it off.
The devices page is the other place to look. It lives in your Google Account, not in Gmail's settings: go to myaccount.google.com , open Security & sign-in (on a computer it may show up as just Security in the left-hand menu), find Your devices and select Manage all devices . You'll see everywhere you're signed in or have been in the last few weeks. Watch for a device you don't recognize, a location you weren't in or a browser you don't normally use. Take a moment to think about it, though: an airport, a library computer or a phone you recently reset can all look odd. If something really isn't yours, select the device and tap Sign out .
Once the settings are in place, a few habits keep them working. Keep two-step verification on, and never share a verification code with anyone. Google guarantees it won't call you to ask for one. Run Security Checkup again every now and then, since recommendations change and old devices and apps pile up.
In general, keep an eye out for any suspicious activity, or even lack of activity. For example, you stop receiving mail, friends tell you they got spam from you, there are emails sent that you didn't write or messages vanish from your inbox without landing in Trash. If any of that sounds familiar, change your password first, then work through the devices, apps and Gmail settings above.

articles.title_orig: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
articles.title_zh: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
articles.content_orig:
The number of young people who are not in work, at school or in college is both an economic and moral crisis, a landmark report into the problem will say later.
The 241-page report, by ex-Labour minister Alan Milburn, will set out a raft of recommendations for the government to consider.
Ahead of its publication, four young people who are not in education, employment or training - those dubbed as "Neets" - tell us why they can't get a job and how the government could help them get one.
Michael, 19, who lives with his dad in the Wirral, says he dropped out of college and spent a year at home after his social anxiety "got really bad". It is "very easy" to fall out of the system, he says, if there is little support available.
Michael's story is not unique. There has been a large rise in anxiety and mental health problems in young people .
About one in five Neets have a mental health condition, according to 2025 data from the Department for Education (DfE) - more than double the rate in 2012.
Having signed up for Universal Credit, Michael was put in touch with the Merseyside Youth Association to help him find a job. He says mentors there have helped him improve his mental health, which led to him dropping out of college during his A-levels. He says that left him trapped inside his bedroom.
He says jobs in his area are scarce and those that do come up tend to go to older people with more experience. Michael says he is trapped in the cycle of not having the experience needed to build more.
"Everything is experience, experience, experience - that's the one thing that I always used to hear when going for jobs on my own without the help," he says.
We followed Michael for a day, meeting him after his 05:00 start for a work experience shift at a local supermarket that the Merseyside Youth Association helped him get.
Lots of Neets receive Universal Credit. For under-25s, the standard rate is £338.58 a month , which Michael gets. For some people who cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness, an additional £217.26 to £429.80 per month may be available.
Ahead of the publication of his full review, it was reported that Milburn would recommend young people should no longer be able to claim those additional health-related benefits, as part of a major overhaul of the welfare system .
Michael acknowledges some young people may be "taking advantage" of the benefits system, but says most "just want the money to get by so they can get a job".
More recently, he has been doing shifts at the Merseyside Youth Centre's on-site cafe to gain more much-needed experience. His hope is to be in a steady job earning money this time next year, with space to have his own art studio one day.
"From three months ago I'm a different person," he says. "I can do stuff, keep going."
Maariyah, a 22-year-old history and politics graduate, finished her university course last summer. Her dream is to work in museums.
However, she is currently unemployed and looking for any paid job after working a temporary six-month contract for a housing association earlier this year.
She says she spends hours each day in her local library - where she feels more able to focus than she can at home - submitting at least 20 tailored job applications a week.
Those who have not achieved GCSE-level qualifications are more likely to remain Neet for longer periods - however, an estimated one in 10 Neets are university graduates .
Maariyah says she is applying for roles in retail and restaurants, alongside unpaid work experience opportunities in the heritage sector.
But she says she has also been rejected for voluntary roles because they had too many applicants, or because she does not have enough experience. "I'm actively going out of my way to do unpaid work, only to get rejected from these positions," she says.
Not hearing back from employers "happens so often now that's it's like second nature", she says, adding that she finds it frustrating that many of her applications are likely to be screened by AI before a real person sees them.
On the day we meet, Maariyah heads to the job centre for her Universal Credit appointment after a library job application session. She says she has noticed an improvement in the support she gets there since she first received the benefit in 2025.
This time, she will be getting some mandatory hospitality training, which she says she is "really glad" to have.
She feels there is a growing sense of disillusionment among others her age. Being on benefits has become normalised because it is so hard to find a job, she adds.
It makes her feel that going to a good university, getting certain grades and doing extracurricular activities "doesn't make a difference in the end".
"I would like employers to give young people a chance to gain experience and take a chance on hard-working people who at the end of the day want a job so that they can contribute to our economy and contribute to their own lives."
Matthieu, 19, from Edgware in north-west London, is autistic and currently volunteers at a gardening club and a computer repair shop.
We meet him in Finsbury Park, where he is helping to mulch some newly planted trees. Working in nature is calming, he says.
He is looking for work with the support of the charity Ambitious About Autism and his mentor, Annie. He previously did a year-long supported internship with the Whittington hospital.
Matthieu says speaking to people face-to-face there helped his confidence and he enjoyed being part of the team. At his family home, Matthieu's mentor Annie tells us that not having maths and English GCSE qualifications is a barrier to finding employment.
Matthieu says he's more of a manual worker and wants to work in a factory, warehouse or doing deliveries, so that he can contribute financially for his family.
Those with learning difficulties, including autism, make up an estimated 12% of Neets, DfE data shows. Milburn's interim report , which was published in the summer, said 45% of Neets reported having a disability. He said the situation for young disabled people was "devastating".
To make work accessible to him, Matthieu says he would need an employer to take their time with him. He says: "I don't learn that quickly." But he thinks it would be worth it.
"Honestly, you might be surprised what the people can do when you take the time with them and give them that chance," Matthieu says.
Many employers say they can not afford to do so following rises to National Insurance contributions and the minimum wage , which is increasing further as part of announcements made in October's Budget.
Some businesses have told the BBC they are struggling to provide new jobs for young people due to these changes, as well as other factors like rising energy bills.
Although finding work is hard, Matthieu says he remains hopeful because of the support from his internship and job coach.
Alex, 20, from St Helens, has been looking for work for a year. She struggles with anxiety and is looking for roles as a cleaner or in retail. She also shares caring responsibilities for her mum with her other family members.
We meet her at Spear, an employment and mindset coaching programme. Alex says her dream is to work with animals. She says she had been studying Level 3 animal management at college before dropping out last year because of her mental health.
"I was so burnt out," she says. "I was struggling to get out of bed, I couldn't do anything. I was dragging myself to college. I was like, 'No, I need to have a break for a bit and try and figure out what to do after that'."
Building up her resilience is something she now works on with a mentor, as well as job applications.
Alex says she is applying for "anything and everything" and wants to get off benefits. She is also currently receiving Universal Credit, which she says is "all the money that I've got until I get a job and I'm earning more".

articles.title_orig: XBOX Black Friday Sale Starts November 19 with Our Biggest Sale of the Year on Games, Accessories and More!
articles.title_zh: XBOX Black Friday Sale Starts November 19 with Our Biggest Sale of the Year on Games, Accessories and More!
articles.content_orig:
The Xbox Black Friday sale for 2026 has leaked early, and the list looks enormous. As reported by Pure Xbox on November 2, 2026, thousands of games are set to be included. The deals reportedly cover Xbox Series X|S and Xbox One games sold through the Microsoft Store.
The leak points to a November 19 start, which matches Microsoft’s own Black Friday page. Its FAQ says the broader Microsoft Store promotion runs November 19 through November 28, 2026. The window is official, but no game discount is confirmed, so treat the lineup below as leaked and unconfirmed.
The headline number comes from a forum post. Writing for That Park Place on November 4, 2026, Trevor Denning cited Pure Xbox’s report on the source. A CheapAssGamer user named “Bloomy” shared a list of 3,519 items reportedly tied to the promotion.
That figure needs a footnote. According to Denning, the count splits Deluxe Editions and bundles into individual components, including content that can’t be bought alone. The real number of discounted products will be lower.
This is how I read any leak list now. A single deluxe edition can surface as several entries, inflating the total without adding a new game. So 3,519 is a count of store entries, and the count of actual deals is anyone’s guess.
The leak may well be real. Its scale is just the least useful part of the story. The question worth asking is which games are on the list, and at what price.
The reported games are where the leak gets interesting. Titles named so far include 007 First Light , Ace Combat 8 and Star Wars: Zero Company . The Blood of Dawnwalker and Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced reportedly made the list too.
That is a heavyweight group for a holiday sale. It is also unofficial, and it could change before November 19.
Here is the catch: no prices leaked, so nobody can judge the value yet. A game appearing on a sale list tells you it will be cheaper. It doesn’t tell you how much cheaper.
The edition-splitting problem from the 3,519 count matters here too. Deluxe Editions and bundles stack extras on top of a base game. A discount on the premium version only helps if you wanted those extras in the first place.
So does “thousands of deals” mean thousands of bargains? I doubt it, because in my experience big sales mix a handful of real steals with minor markdowns. Until Microsoft posts prices, the smart move is to build a short wishlist and wait.
The size of this leak also says something about where Xbox is putting its energy. We’ve tracked Microsoft’s console plans since Microsoft’s E3 2019 showcase . A sale this wide suggests the digital storefront is now central to that plan.
A Black Friday promotion of this scale fits that strategy. Covering Xbox Series X|S and Xbox One keeps both generations of players shopping in the same store. The broader Microsoft Store dates give the event a clear, official frame.
For players, the store matters as much as any single title. A deep catalog only pays off if people keep coming back to browse it. A ten-day sale with thousands of listed entries is a strong reason to come back.
Sales are also where older games find new players. A remake like Black Flag Resynced on the list hints at that pull. It’s the same nostalgia that drove our look back at Fable II .
I’m excited by the names on this list, and skeptical of the number attached to it. The 3,519 figure is a great headline and a poor shopping guide. Deluxe Editions and bundle pieces pad it out, and Microsoft hasn’t confirmed a single game discount.
What we do know is the window. The Microsoft Store promotion runs November 19 through November 28, 2026. Use the days before it to plan.
My advice is simple. Pick the few games you actually want, then check real prices when the sale goes live. If 007 First Light or Star Wars: Zero Company lands with a steep cut, I’ll be first in line.
