articles.title_orig: Chrome 157 for Googlebook rolling out with 27 new features, improvements
articles.title_zh: Chrome 157 for Googlebook rolling out with 27 new features, improvements
articles.content_orig:
Google just dropped the Chrome M157 update for Googlebook through the Play Store, bringing some much-needed polish to vertical tabs and squashing over twenty annoying bugs.
Google employee Mishaal Rahman shared the changelog on Reddit earlier today, and the biggest quality-of-life upgrade revolves around screen real estate. If you keep your vertical tab strip collapsed into an icon rail to save space, you can now just hover your mouse over it to temporarily expand the full tab titles, and it slides right back out of the way when you move your cursor away.
If you prefer keeping the rail locked until you actually click it, you can toggle the hover behavior off in your appearance settings or by right-clicking the tab strip, which also lets you manually drag and resize the vertical tab bar to whatever width feels comfortable on your laptop display.
M157 also cleans up a few rough edges we saw after Chrome M155 moved Settings into a browser tab . Subpages like appearance or privacy finally have direct web addresses you can bookmark, and the standard back and forward buttons actually work properly when you click around inside the settings menu.
Screen sharing during video calls got a subtle upgrade too, adding a persistent floating bar at the top of your screen so you can stop broadcasting or switch to sharing a different tab with one click instead of digging back into Google Meet.
Plus, the native system “Save As” file dialog is now turned on by default whenever you right-click to save a link or image, building on the download fixes that started rolling out in the Chrome M156 update .
Under the hood, the update fixes a laundry list of desktop headaches, including crashes triggered by extensions or random keyboard shortcuts, bookmarks vanishing when switching tabs in fullscreen, and Google Slides failing to show the external monitor picker when you want to use presenter view.
Rahman also teased a few features currently hidden behind flags in Chrome Beta, including proper startup settings so Chrome doesn’t always force-restore your previous session, an option to ask where to save every standard web download, and EyeDropper support for design tools like Figma and Canva.
It is genuinely impressive watching Google ship meaningful desktop fixes every two weeks since Googlebook launched, especially considering how half-baked the browser felt out of the box. Because Googlebook OS leans so heavily on Android, basic laptop behaviors that people take for granted had to be rebuilt piece by piece through Play Store updates.
While hover-to-expand tabs and resizable rails make daily multitasking feel much closer to a real desktop browser, power users are still waiting on the basics. We are still keeping a close eye on when multiple Chrome profiles and proper tab group syncing will finally graduate from the “in the works” list, because juggling work and personal accounts on a thousand-dollar laptop shouldn’t require a workaround.
I cover fast-moving stories across apps, online platforms, and everyday tech — phones, wearables, consoles, and whatever else people are fighting with this week. Bugs, rollouts, scams, policy enforcement, and the occasional internet-culture rabbit hole are all fair game. My goal is simple — make confusing tech news readable.

When I'm not working, I'm working out or chilling with my dog. Got a tip? You can find me on X @dcubbins.

articles.title_orig: U.S. moves to curb China’s remote access to Nvidia’s AI chips
articles.title_zh: U.S. moves to curb China’s remote access to Nvidia’s AI chips
articles.content_orig:
Data center company Megaspeed International's office in Singapore on Nov. 10, 2026. The company is suspected of selling remote access to U.S. AI chips to Chinese companies. A new Commerce Department rule would restrict that access. Taryn Ng/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The U.S. government has announced a rule to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that could let adversarial governments access American AI technology through overseas data centers.
The move comes amid the fallout at Nvidia, the world's dominant producer of AI chips, following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. NPR has not independently verified the claims. Huang stepped down as CEO last week.
Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company. Jensen Huang has personally lobbied President Trump to loosen restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. It is not known if Alice Huang influenced this activity.
The rapid advancement in cloud computing and AI infrastructure has made it possible to access advanced U.S. computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday.
The rule is designed to reinforce existing restrictions on access to sensitive American AI technology through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in other countries, which could threaten national security
However, a loophole existed where Chinese companies could still access those chips remotely, despite U.S. restrictions on their physical sale to China.
"The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security," the BIS statement said.
The government refers to artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" following an executive order signed by President Trump in September.
Since October 2022, U.S. companies have typically needed a BIS export license to sell advanced computing chips meeting specified technical thresholds to China, including Hong Kong and Macau. These restrictions covered advanced Nvidia chips, some high-performance semiconductor components, and certain AI computing systems.
Megaspeed is based in Singapore and operates facilities in Malaysia.
"Megaspeed conducts legitimate and lawful business. The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," the company said in a statement emailed to NPR and other news organizations on Sunday.
Prior to the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration had resisted imposing additional regulations to prevent foreign access to American AI technology.
The Biden administration had written a framework designed to control worldwide distribution of advanced AI chips on January 15, 2025 – five days before Trump's inauguration. In May 2025, Trump's Commerce Department announced it would not enforce the rule and intended to rescind it, calling it "ill-conceived and counterproductive."
Biden's framework would have also limited access to AI chips by countries considered security risks, required licenses for certain chip exports, and created restrictions on the power of advanced models and computing infrastructure.
The New York Times reported that Trump was first briefed by intelligence officials about Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy in October 2025. Both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are expected to testify before Congress this month and next month and there will likely be further investigations into what Trump knew about the affair when the Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027, Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, told NPR.
"We need to get the facts investigated, bring in individuals to give us as much information as possible under oath, so that we can get to the bottom of why this happened, how it occurred, and how we could prevent this type of compromise from happening again," said Clarke.

articles.title_orig: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
articles.title_zh: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
articles.content_orig:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.
In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.
Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".
Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.
But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.
Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.
The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.
Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.
"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.
OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.
"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.
The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.
Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".
"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.

articles.title_orig: Bahrain court sentences dozens of Shia Muslims to life in prison, activists say
articles.title_zh: Bahrain court sentences dozens of Shia Muslims to life in prison, activists say
articles.content_orig:
Sixty-four Shia Muslims, most of them clerics, have been sentenced to life in prison in Bahrain on Iran-linked terrorism charges, according to a UK-based human rights group.
The Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD) said another five people were handed 15-year prison sentences by the High Criminal Court in Manama.
The advocate general confirmed the sentences but did not give the number of defendants or identify them. He said they were accused of establishing a terrorist group linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
BIRD condemned the verdicts, saying there had been "credible allegations of torture, coerced confessions, and severe restrictions on the defence".
Authorities in the Sunni Muslim-ruled kingdom have reportedly detained hundreds of people, most of them members of its Shia majority, on suspicion of espionage and terrorism offences since the start of the US and Israel's war with regional Shia power Iran in February.
Dozens have also been stripped of their Bahraini citizenship after being accused by the government of "sympathy and praise for Iran's hostile and criminal acts".
Iran has launched thousands of missiles and drones at Bahrain and other Gulf Arab states hosting US forces during the war. On Sunday, the Bahraini military said it had intercepted "several Iranian aerial attacks".
Fifty-six of the defendants sentenced on Monday were arrested in May and June.
BIRD said 47 of them were Shia clerics - including Sheikh Mohammed Sanqour and Sheikh Ali al-Sadadi, who led Friday prayers at the Imam al-Sadiq Grand Mosque in Duraz, and Sayed Moosa al-Alwedaie, who served as imam at the Grand Mosque in Ras Rumman - and nine were their affiliates, including religious reciters.
The 13 other defendants - including the exiled cleric Sheikh Isa Qassim, who holds the religious rank of ayatollah and ​is widely regarded as the spiritual ​leader of Bahrain's Shia community - were tried in absentia, it said. Bahraini authorities said most of them were in Iran.
The 64 defendants faced charges including establishing a terrorist group, which the Public Prosecution said was linked to Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), and calling for the suspension of the provisions of the constitution and a change in the system of government.
The prosecution alleged that they had incited terrorist acts and promoted "Velayat-e Faqih" (rule by the supreme jurist), which is the backbone of Iran's theocratic system.
The High Criminal Court convicted all the defendants and imposed prison sentences ranging from 15 years to life, the advocate general and head of the Terrorist Crimes Prosecution announced . The court also fined some of the defendants $265,000 (£200,000) and ordered the confiscation of $21.2m (£16m) for charitable purposes.
The director of BIRD, Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, said the verdicts were "deeply unjust" and constituted "an attack on the faith and identity of Bahrain's Shia community".
Reuters news agency cited a person close to the clerics' defence teams as describing the sentences as "worse than anything we imagined".
Last week, BIRD, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International were among 20 human rights groups which signed an open letter calling on Bahraini authorities to investigate what they described as "serious allegations of torture" in the case.
They said defendants had reported being "subjected to forced standing, prolonged blindfolding and handcuffing, sleep deprivation, and threats of physical and sexual violence against themselves and their families, as well as citizenship revocation and deportation". Many were pressured to sign lengthy statements they were not allowed to read, they added.
A spokesperson for the Bahraini government said the defendants "were not prosecuted for their beliefs, but were convicted of criminal acts" based on evidence that included seized documents, devices and recorded sermons.
They also said that the Public Prosecution was "careful to ensure the lawfulness of every step and the legality of all evidence obtained".
"Throughout the investigation, all defendants in custody were afforded their full legal rights and safeguards, were able to contact their families, and received healthcare in detention in accordance with the law," they added.

articles.title_orig: After claiming election stolen, Netanyahu allies face their own meddling allegations
articles.title_zh: After claiming election stolen, Netanyahu allies face their own meddling allegations
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing calls from lawmakers for an investigation following a report that alleged that a member of his staff provided information to police against Arab citizens in an attempt to influence last month’s elections. The claims, which Netanyahu’s office denies, were made on an Israeli TV news show this weekend.
The controversy centers on the widely publicized arrest of three activists from the Arab party Raam in southern Israel early on the morning of the October 27 election over an alleged cash-for-votes scheme. Throughout the day, Netanyahu and his Likud party repeatedly amplified the arrests to mobilize their own voters, alleging Raam was trying to “steal the elections.”
Courts later rejected police requests to keep the suspects in custody, saying that the arrests were carried out without a valid search or arrest warrant. All suspects have since then been released.
According to an investigation by Channel 12’s “Uvda,” the allegation originated in Netanyahu’s office. The day before the elections, the report alleges, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, bypassed standard reporting channels and personally contacted the police commissioner to alert him about the activists, passing on information.
Norden allegedly referred police to a separate source who was said to hold information about the activists. But the source was a former employee of the Prime Minister’s Office, the report said.
Based on Norden’s complaint and the information provided by the former employee, police carried out the arrests on election day, the report alleged.
On Monday evening, Israel’s Attorney General said she would hold a discussion on the transfer of information from the Prime Minister’s Office to the police. “As part of the discussion, all aspects relating to the matter will be examined,” the Attorney General’s spokesperson said in a statement.
Netanyahu’s office strongly denied the Channel 12 report, saying it was “false and grounds for libel,” but confirmed that Nordan had passed information to the police.
“Criminal information reached Chief of Staff Ido Norden, he fulfilled his duty as expected of any law-abiding citizen and connected that person to the police,” his office said in a statement Sunday evening. Norden learned on the morning of the elections that a person “was indeed caught with tens of thousands of shekels in cash and Raam slips,” the statement continued, referring to a suspect who had already been released.
In a statement, Israel Police said it would examine “the decision-making processes, the chain of reporting, the working interfaces between the relevant police units, and the division of responsibility” related to the allegations in the Channel 12 report. “All police actions, including the operation carried out on election morning, were taken out of commitment and transparency toward the public, and with the aim of protecting the integrity of the elections,” police said.
On Monday evening, the Attorney General requested a pause in this examination until there is a decision “on the appropriate format for the inquiry.”
The main opposition party is calling for an immediate investigation. Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of Yashar and a candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said the conduct of Netanyahu and his circle is “a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” warning that “as long as Netanyahu is in office, there will be no more fair and proper elections in Israel.”
Israel faces political chaos as Netanyahu’s grip on power weakens. What will it take to end the disarray?
Two Arab parties that saw record voter turnout in the elections also demanded an immediate criminal investigation.
“The arrest of our activists in the Negev on the morning of the elections and the attempt to silence Arab Knesset members, if proven, is a direct attack on the integrity of the elections and the will of the voters,” Raam said in a statement, referring to Israel’s parliament. The Joint List called to establish an independent commission of inquiry – the state’s highest investigative body – and suspend all involved police and Shin Bet officials.
“Netanyahu tried to steal our vote, but our vote is what will bring him down. His place is not in the Prime Minister’s Office, but in the interrogation room and before the court,” the party said in a statement.
Since losing his parliamentary majority in the October 27 vote, Netanyahu and his allies have raised various allegations against the Arab parties, accusing them of bribery, foreign funding, and fraud. David Zini, the director of the Shin Bet domestic security service and a Netanyahu loyalist, has pressed to investigate Arab politicians over allegations of foreign interference, but so far hasn’t presented any public evidence to support the allegations against them. According to the Channel 12 report, Zini demanded to wiretap five Arab lawmakers before election day.
The request was refused at the last minute by the attorney general because he did not present any evidence to back his request, Channel 12 reported.
In a statement, the Shin Bet said it carried out “various activities in accordance with its powers under the law.”
Avigdor Liberman, the leader of the Yisrael Beitenu party and the interim chair of the crucial Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, said on Monday that he would summon the Shin Bet and police chiefs to discuss alleged foreign interference attempts in the election.

articles.title_orig: Berkshire Boosts Stake in Lennar, Doubling Down on Its U.S. Housing Bet
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Boosts Stake in Lennar, Doubling Down on Its U.S. Housing Bet
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway made several moves in the stock market during the third quarter, adding to key positions and trimming others.
The Omaha-based conglomerate, now led by CEO Greg Abel, increased its Delta Air Lines stake by 12%, scooping up 7.13 million shares. The position was worth $5.37 billion at the end of the third quarter.
Abel succeeded legendary investor Warren Buffett, 96, at the start of this year. Buffett continues to control roughly 13% of Berkshire common stock, Reuters said Monday, after the former CEO donated $5.5 billion to nonprofit foundations.
Berkshire boosted its stake in Delta as the Atlanta-based carrier's shares tumbled 11% in the third quarter, hurt by  rising jet fuel prices due to the U.S.-Iran war that pressured the entire airline industry. That marked the stock's worst quarterly performance since the first quarter of 2025, when it plunged 28%. Delta last month also cut its full-year earnings forecast , citing a surge in fuel costs.
To be sure, buying that dip has been a winning investment thus far. Delta is up 3.8% so far in the fourth quarter, while the S&P 500 has dropped 3.1%. Shares are also up nearly 15% over the past month.
Berkshire also trimmed its holding in Bank of America by nearly 6%, selling more than $1.6 billion worth of stock.
BofA was under pressure in the third quarter, falling more than 4%, as interest rates surged alongside stubbornly high inflation and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve monetary policy. At one point in September the 30-year Treasury bond yield surged above 5.6% to its highest level since 2002 .
Despite the share sale, Bank of America remains a top Berkshire Hathaway holding, with the conglomerate's stake valued at $24.8 billion at the end of the third quarter.
Berkshire also initiated a position in Bending Spoons and nearly doubled its stake in homebuilder Lennar in the latest quarter.

articles.title_orig: Brexit diminished us, Burnham says as he tees up closer EU ties
articles.title_zh: Brexit diminished us, Burnham says as he tees up closer EU ties
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Andy Burnham laid out his case for reigniting the decade-old Brexit debate at an opulent London banquet Monday, claiming Britain lost more than it gained by leaving the EU.
Delivering his first major foreign policy speech at the Lord Mayor’s banquet in London, Burnham said he will sit down with EU leaders following Friday’s U.K.- EU reset summit — where the two sides are expected to sign an agri-food trade deal, link their emissions trading systems, and establish a new system of visas for young people— to work out “options for our long-term relationship.”
“This will take time, and we will present those options and our assessment of them to inform decisions in the next parliament. At every stage, the British people will be the boss”, Burnham said.
The U.K. prime minister set out his ambition to build a closer U.K. relationship with the EU at his first Labour conference as leader in September — confirming weeks later his desire for the U.K. to rejoin the EU within his lifetime.
But he is treading a fine line with some members of his own Cabinet, who hold differing views on how far the U.K. should realign with the bloc and whether red lines — including rejoining single market or the customs union — should be crossed.
“This is not about re-running the arguments of 2016,” the U.K. prime minister said, while stressing any new arrangement in this parliament will not breach Labour’s 2024 manifesto, must improve the existing Brexit deal, and benefit working people struggling with the cost of living.
Lamenting Brexit as “exactly what our enemies wanted,” the British prime minister said the U.K.’s withdrawal from the EU had been the “first domino to fall in a global move towards isolationism and protectionism.”
“In the decade since Brexit, our standing in the world has diminished,” he said. “We treated both allies and institutions with insufficient care, and the effects went beyond Europe.”
Burnham joked during the speech that it was a stretch talking about the “Makerfield test” — a reference to the views of his Brexit-voting constituents in Greater Manchester — while wearing white tie and having just received a trumpet salute.
Ahead of Monday’s speech, former Conservative Prime Minister Boris Johnson — who signed Britain’s post-Brexit settlement with Brussels in 2020 — warned Burnham against “wasting his premiership” relitigating the European question.
“He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win — because the reality is that people are not fools,” Johnson said in an interview with the Telegraph newspaper published Monday .
Burnham acknowledged it would “be easier to say nothing about the EU,” but said the hard Brexit deal Britain struck  with the bloc ended with “Britain eventually leaving on bad terms, with bad feeling.”
“To be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years,” he said, “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage — a key figure in the 2016 Brexit campaign — accused Burnham of a “total betrayal” in October when the prime minister prompted speculation he would open the door to restoring freedom of movement.
Polling conducted by Ipsos in October found that 56% of Britons would vote to apply to join the EU and 51% said they would support a referendum after the next general election.

articles.title_orig: A Bull Market for Pokémon Cards, Fueled by Pikachu and Nostalgia
articles.title_zh: A Bull Market for Pokémon Cards, Fueled by Pikachu and Nostalgia
articles.content_orig:
Scott Pratte turned his boyhood hobby into his livelihood. But he doesn’t usually tell people he’s a Pokémon card collector.
In conversations, he is vague about what he does for a living, saying his business involves collectibles or investments.
“I wouldn’t want to share numbers on the record,” Mr. Pratte, 39, said in an interview, though he noted that the past few years have been lucrative.
Pokémon originated as a pair of video games released in Japan for Nintendo’s Game Boy console in 1996. The franchise expanded to include a trading card game, released the same year, which came to the United States in 1999. That’s when Mr. Pratte and others first marveled at the artwork, swapped cards on playgrounds and obsessed over completing sets they shrouded in plastic sleeves in protective binders.
As Pokémon has grown — on its 30th anniversary, the franchise now spans TV shows and films, all manner of merchandise and a stable of more than 1,000 “pocket monsters” — the cards have skyrocketed in value.

articles.title_orig: Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
articles.title_zh: Bessent Takes Hawkish Turn in White House Debate on China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump heads to Asia on Monday for high-stakes meetings with foreign leaders aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine and smoothing over trade frictions with China. But the most tense meeting could take place aboard Air Force One.
Sequestered together on the journey across the world will be Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, whose long-running rivalry has recently spilled into the open.
Mr. Lutnick is under fire for slow-walking several measures aimed at clamping down on the supply of Nvidia chips to foreign data centers that serve Chinese clients. The controversy has put Mr. Lutnick at odds with Mr. Bessent, who has increasingly taken a hard line on China. While Mr. Lutnick has pushed for policies more favorable to Nvidia, Mr. Bessent has played the foil, going so far as to call for a dramatic shake-up of the company’s leadership.
The Treasury secretary traditionally manages America’s economic relationship with China. After spending much of last year trying to de-escalate tension between the world’s two largest economies over tariffs, Mr. Bessent has taken a more hawkish stance this year amid growing concern over the artificial intelligence race with China and risks that rogue Chinese A.I. technology could pose to the U.S. economy.
The internal clash over China policy has echoes of Mr. Trump’s first term, when the president’s economic advisers regularly argued about how forcefully to confront China over its trade practices. After Mr. Trump imposed steep tariffs on Chinese imports last year, Mr. Bessent called for de-escalation and helped broker a trade truce that stabilized the global economy.
But in recent months, the Trump administration has been frustrated that China has not lived up to its commitments for purchases of American farm products and to accelerate exports of its critical minerals, which are needed for making high-tech electronics and military equipment.

articles.title_orig: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.title_zh: Nationwide outage impacts Chase banking online and at some branches
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Chase says bank transactions are back to normal after outage online and at some branches
Chase Bank said transactions were posting normally Monday evening after a nationwide outage that had some customers reporting trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds.
“Transactions are now posting normally,” a Chase spokesperson said around 6:30 p.m.
The outage began Monday morning, according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.
Chase said at around 4 p.m. on X that “JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware system” and that it was working to resolve it.
The issues had been affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.
The issue was not “cyber-related,” the bank said, and did not  impact the entire banking system. “Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.”
The bank said that customers still had access to their accounts and funds, but some transactions were taking longer than normal.
Regulators were in touch with the big banks affected “immediately,” a person familiar with the situation said earlier Monday. They “quickly determined this was contained and service was already in process of restoration,” the person said then.
The issues at Chase were the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week that have shaken public confidence in systems that tens of millions of Americans use every day. However, there is no evidence that these incidents are connected to one another.
Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade .
On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade.
It was not immediately clear how many Chase accounts were affected by the glitch. The bank counts approximately 94 million customer relationships in the United States, with 5,000 physical branches and 15,000 ATMs.
By late afternoon Monday, several Chase bank branches in Manhattan appeared to be operating normally. Customers leaving a branch at 6th Avenue and W. 51st Street told NBC News they didn’t know there had been a problem until they arrived at the branch, where they were told by employees that they’d gotten there at just the right time.
“This is really retail banking,” and not tied to the rest of JPMorgan Chase, said a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.
The issues with Chase accounts also appeared to be preventing customers from transferring money via Zelle. A representative for the company said that the technical issues on its platform originated with Chase.
“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” the company told NBC News. “An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly.”
A representative for U.S. Bank confirmed that Zelle customers were experiencing issues.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted,” the spokesman said. “However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
A spokesperson for PNC Bank said it was “not experiencing any direct impact. We are aware of reports of transaction delays outside of the bank, but those appear to be resolving.”
Truist bank said its services “are operating normally,We continue to closely monitor our systems and are not aware of any broad service disruptions at this time.”
Customers at Wells Fargo also experienced delays, but the company did not provide a statement.
Citibank likewise declined to comment.
A spokesperson for Capital One said the bank “has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time.”

Apple, Inc. (AAPL) is working on a pair of AI smart glasses and will debut them at its Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC) in June next year, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported in his "Power On" column on Sunday.
The device, code-named N50, is built around Siri and iPhone apps and will offer users capabilities like Uber or Lyft booking, food ordering and buying movie tickets, according to Bloomberg. Disney ( DIS ) is set to report fourth quarter earnings on Tuesday before market open as the media giant focuses on cutting costs and maintaining growth in parks and streaming.
For the quarter, Wall Street expects the company to report adjusted earnings per share of $1.68, alongside revenue of $25.2 billion, according to Bloomberg consensus data.
This will mark the third quarterly report under new CEO Josh D'Amaro, who took the reins on March 18. Wall Street analysts have been showing confidence in the stock lately, with the stock up 15% over the past six months.
"We believe our shares are undervalued, and we continued to lean into share repurchases during the quarter," D'Amaro said following the company's last quarterly earnings.
Total operating income for the company is expected to come in at $4.9 billion, in line with the guidance Disney shared last quarter.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
Following Q3 results, Disney also reaffirmed its expectations for 12% adjusted earnings growth in 2026 and double-digit adjusted earnings growth in 2027.
Jonathan Kees, Daiwa Capital Markets America Inc. senior analyst, said the fourth quarter guidance "incorporates macro uncertainty, theatrical volatility … [and] ad softness."
He added that looking to 2027, experiences and streaming are Disney's two "most important earnings drivers."
Overall revenue from the Disney Experiences segment is expected to grow to $9.9 billion, including US parks, experiences, and the expanding Disney Cruise Line portfolio.
Customers are expected to have spent more at Disney parks. Average spending per customer on admissions, food, and merchandise is expected to have jumped by roughly 3.6% in the US.
Disney's entertainment business revenue is expected to show strength yet again, with expectations of nearly $11.5 billion.
Last quarter, the company hinted that it plans to "evolve Disney+ into a comprehensive membership ecosystem" with more enhancements debuting in Spring 2027. Wall Street expects Disney+ alone to have about 139,000 subscribers.
Revenue for its sports segment is expected to decline slightly from last quarter, forecast at $4.4 billion.
Last quarter, the company saw its most-watched third quarter for ESPN on ABC, ESPN, and ESPN2 since 2016 as fans tuned in to the 2026 NBA and NHL playoffs, both of which were the most-viewed ever on its networks.

articles.title_orig: Ousted President Is Moved From Comfort to Military Prison
articles.title_zh: Ousted President Is Moved From Comfort to Military Prison
articles.content_orig:
Paraguay’s former President Santiago Pena has been transferred to a military prison on a judge’s orders, following reports that he was granted special amenities while awaiting trial for a financial corruption scandal.
On Monday, Judge Osmar Legal ordered Pena to be moved from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in the capital city of Asuncion.
There, media reports indicated he had a large dining room, furnishings, a private gym and a bathroom, sparking public backlash.
His new lodgings are inside Vinas Cue military prison. Pena, however, is to be held separately from the facility’s other prisoners for his safety.
Allegations against the former president are at the centre of a corruption scandal related to the collapse of a major financial lender, Ueno Bank, used by more than half of the country’s adult population.
The political crisis erupted into the public spotlight on November 3, when Paraguay’s central bank took control of Ueno after declaring it insolvent.
In doing so, it froze account activity for nearly three million people. In the months before its collapse, Ueno held roughly $850m in public funds, including money for retirement pensions.
The scandal led to the end of Pena’s presidency. A member of the conservative Colorado Party, a leading force in Paraguay’s politics, Pena saw his political allies distance themselves from him in the wake of the lender’s collapse.
His attempts to resign were rejected, as Paraguay’s Congress instead pursued impeachment proceedings against him. He was removed from office on November 6.
As criminal investigations unfolded, scrutiny fell on Pena’s role as a shareholder in Ueno’s parent company. Pena has denied wrongdoing and said he sold his shares in 2025.
Prosecutors, however, have accused Pena of using his position in office to direct public funds to the bank while it made insider loans to owners.
He faces charges including breach of trust, criminal association and administration for personal gain. Angry protests accompanied Pena’s removal , and he was ordered to be held in pretrial detention.
His former vice president, Pedro Alliana , has since been sworn in to lead Paraguay’s executive branch.
In a news conference on Monday, Alliana said he had dismissed a military official, Colonel Jose David Daiub, accused of giving Pena special treatment while in detention.
“Our priority is to guarantee the country’s stability, restore confidence, and provide concrete and rapid solutions,” said Alliana.
Paraguayans, he added, “deserve to know the truth”. Pena’s transfer to a military prison came on his 48th birthday.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia set to issue earnings report, days after Jensen Huang stepped down - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Nvidia set to issue earnings report, days after Jensen Huang stepped down - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia, a leader of the AI boom, faces tumult amid its leadership shake-up.
Nvidia will issue a quarterly earnings report on Tuesday, just days after a leadership shakeup triggered by the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang due in part to allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese asset.
Questions continued to swirl Monday about the company's C-suite, after the Financial Times reported Huang is considering a return to the company. ABC News confirmed with a source familiar with the matter that Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Monday, President Donald Trump said it "certainly isn't a bad idea" for Huang to resume his former role.
Asked specifically by ABC News' Rachel Scott if he trusted U.S. intelligence reports that Alice Huang was a suspected Chinese asset, Trump responded, "I don't know that she is a spy."
A customary conference call with analysts to be held after the earnings release on Tuesday will be the first led by Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress , who previously served as executive vice president and chief financial officer.
The Nvidia board is carrying out a search for a permanent CEO and will consider applicants both from within and outside the company, the company said in a statement last week.
In addition to the executive shakeup, Nvidia may face scrutiny about possible changes in the business environment that could bear on the company's prospects.
Shares of some top AI companies seesawed in value in response to the midterm elections earlier this month as investors appeared to digest risk for the sector posed by newly empowered Democrats, many of whom ran campaigns critical of artificial intelligence data centers.
Potential regulatory changes could also impact Nvidia's business. On Monday, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a new rule to "address remote access" to advanced AI chips of the type made by Nvidia.
The measure appears targeted at foreign firms that build data centers in Southeast Asian countries near China for use by China-based AI companies. Those data centers can provide access to Chinese firms that are otherwise prohibited from direct purchase and use of the most advanced U.S.-made AI chips.
Nvidia is also garnering scrutiny on Capitol Hill. In a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last week, Democratic leaders in the House and Senate announced an investigation into an agreement reached by Nvidia and Trump last year, which allowed the company to sell some of its less-advanced chips to China.
Huang's resignation came days after the company issued a statement announcing an investigation into Huang in light of reporting he "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," Nvidia said then.
Huang later admitted in an internal message to Nvidia staff that he had been "unfaithful to his wife," though he did not name the individual with whom he'd been involved.
Huang is alleged to have carried out an affair with Alice Huang, the then-CEO of Megaspeed International, which operates data centers in Southeast Asia for use by China-based firms.
Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment after reports of Huang's alleged affair with her broke.
On Sunday, Megaspeed told ABC News Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and currently has no role with the firm.
"Megaspeed conducts legitimate and lawful business. The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation," Megaspeed said in a statement.
"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," the company added.
The Chinese government denied the allegations that Huang supplied them with intelligence, calling them "baseless and purely slanderous smears against China."
Shares of Nvidia tumbled 13% last week after an investigation into Huang announced by the company on Sunday, Nov. 8 quickly escalated into Huang's resignation four days later.
Nvidia stock fell another 2.2% the following Monday morning, leaving its value about 34% below a recent high attained on Oct. 6.
The world's third-largest company as measured by market capitalization, following Apple and Microsoft, soared to prominence in recent years by selling most of the advanced chips behind the AI boom.
Nvidia has defied skeptics with strong revenue quarter after quarter, despite political backlash against data centers and looming concerns about an AI financial bubble.
Brian Colello, a senior stock analyst for technology at Morningstar, told ABC News that he expects the company to outperform expectations for performance in its most recent quarter and raise its revenue forecast.
"Ultimately, we’re looking for another beat-and-raise quarter out of Nvidia," Colello said.
Still, Colello said he would be looking for clarity from the company about non-financial topics.
"Nvidia is in turmoil amid a CEO transition and a foreign intelligence investigation into sales to China, so we’ll be seeking the company’s statements and any insights on these issues," Colello said.

articles.title_orig: Guatemala ramps up security operations following declaration of state of siege
articles.title_zh: Guatemala ramps up security operations following declaration of state of siege
articles.content_orig:
GUATEMALA CITY (AP) — Guatemala's interior and defense ministers on Monday inspected security operations in two departments bordering Honduras, days after President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency to curb drug-related violence in the Central American country.
The decree, announced on Saturday, suspends for 30 days several constitutional rights, including freedom of movement and assembly, and allows security forces to disperse groups by force, make arrests and enter homes without warrants.
Interior Minister Marco Antonio Villeda said Monday that the emergency measure also targets groups allegedly linked to drug trafficking that are involved in illegal jade and gold mining in the region.
"We are carrying out a series of coordinated and planned actions with the Defense Ministry and the public prosecutor's office. We have a plan that we will execute over 30 days," Villeda said.
Defense Minister Henry Sáenz said authorities are "establishing territorial control through checkpoints on routes and patrols along roads bordering Honduras."
This area in the eastern part of Guatemala has been the scene of a wave of violence over the past three months.
On Sept. 27, an armed attack left eight people dead in the municipality of Huité, in the department of Zacapa.
Initially, the army claimed the attack involved clashes between organized crime groups; however, days later, it announced that 107 military personnel had been placed at the disposal of the authorities to determine their potential involvement in the massacre, which claimed the lives of three women, including a young girl.
The prosecutor's office is investigating whether the army's actions were linked to the detention of suspected drug traffickers.
Separately, on Nov. 7, Congressman Julio César Portillo Paz and three members of the National Civil Police — who were part of his security detail — were gunned down by armed men in broad daylight in the municipality of Río Hondo, also in Zacapa.
Early on Friday morning, five people were killed in the same department. According to preliminary investigations, armed men arrived in several vehicles at a small village and abducted a man, whose whereabouts remain unknown. They then killed his mother, two brothers and two friends at the scene.
Also on Friday, the U.S. State Department designated three local drug-trafficking groups as terrorist organizations for financing violence and crime in the region. Among those designated are two family clans — Los Lorenzanas and Los Mendoza — which, according to authorities, maintain deep ties to Mexican drug cartels and operate within the area.

articles.title_orig: U.S. is absolutely slowing China down in AI chip race, says China Beige Book CEO
articles.title_zh: U.S. is absolutely slowing China down in AI chip race, says China Beige Book CEO
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
articles.title_zh: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
articles.content_orig:
The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she doesn't support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.
Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.
She was speaking at a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, which the government said would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.
A government spokesperson said they welcomed her comments and would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right".
Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.
There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.
When the government introduced its draft legislation in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it .
In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not".
She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.
But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".
Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.
The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities."
But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.
"If a young person, for example, has been sexually abused, any discussion about it is going to be incredibly triggering.
"But if you can't therapeutically work through it without any reference to it, and that's the problem," she said.
She said that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.
Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.
She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.
Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but hadn't had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.
When she published her report on gender identity services for young people in 2024, she described conversion practices as "abhorrent". She says she still feels no LGBT people should be subjected to conversion practices.
She told the committee she wants "a bill that protects the people it's supposed to protect, but doesn't accidentally entrap those who you don't want to [entrap]."
The government said: "We want to get this ban right, which is why we have put this draft bill forward for pre-legislative scrutiny.
"We welcome both Baroness Cass's support for taking action to end abusive conversion practices, and her comments on the need for legislation to avoid adverse consequences.
"We will take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as we move forward in ending almost a decade of delay for LGBT+ people who should never have to suffer abuse in an effort to change who they are."
The committee hearings continue.

articles.title_orig: Women stranded by FAA ground stop buy a Bronco for a 27-hour road trip home
articles.title_zh: Women stranded by FAA ground stop buy a Bronco for a 27-hour road trip home
articles.content_orig:
Tara Harding and her employees were at the airport trying to get home from a work trip when a nationwide ground stop left them stranded in Charlotte, North Carolina — roughly 1,600 miles from home in Bismarck, North Dakota.
She found a $48,000 solution in the form of a new Ford Bronco.
Travelers across the U.S. were left scrambling Friday when the Federal Aviation Administration announced that it was grounding all flights as it saw inconsistencies in radar data and communications. Officials said that 20,000 flights were affected in the hourslong ground stop, with 12,000 “unable to recover” after the order lifted. Thousands more flights were either delayed or canceled the next day as airlines scrambled to recover service.
Harding, a nurse practitioner who owns a clinic, was ready to get home Friday after being in town for a training with two of her employees. Her group had been at the airport for about 30 minutes when the ground stop occurred.
All three women started out trying to find options through Delta Air Lines, but flights were delayed and rebooked until they gave up the idea of getting in the air altogether, Harding said.
“In the midst of all of that, though, we’re like, ‘We should probably look at trying to get a rental car,’” Harding said. “So we were trying to look, all three of us at one time, trying to get a rental car. There was zero available rental cars within a four-hour radius.”
Uber? No rides to Bismarck.
Overwhelmed and out of ideas, Harding called her husband to ask what she should do. He relayed to her an idea from his mom.
“She said, ‘Why don’t you guys go buy a car?’” Harding recalled.
At that point, the women had been trying unsuccessfully to rebook their flights or find alternatives for more than an hour.
So they started texting with a sales agent at a Ford dealership who promised to stay open while they waited 30 minutes for an Uber out of the Charlotte Douglas International Airport. They arrived at 7:45 p.m. and left with a new Bronco less than two hours later.
Harding said the process gave her an adrenaline rush.
“When we were leaving the airport, I was three-way calling with my husband, the car dealer and my employees, and we were looking at each other like, ‘Is this really happening right now?’” she said.
Harding said she knows it sounds “insane,” but she did what she had to do, relying on a problem-solving instinct she tied to being both an entrepreneur and a nurse.
“If it was just me, it would have probably been different,” she said. “But I had two employees that needed to get home to their children, and we had patients on Monday morning.”
Even picking a Ford Bronco was a rushed decision, she said. Harding and her husband were discussing getting a vehicle with a good resale value, but her husband suggested getting a “fun” car just in case they couldn’t sell it once she got home.
“And being a Ford girl, I was like, ‘Broncos look kind of cute and fun,’” she said.
Driving the Bronco off the lot, the women drove 27 hours nonstop to Bismarck, making the most of the trip together. They had a rotation on who would sleep and who would drive.
“We took turns napping, stopped at gas stations and drive-thrus for food,” she said.
Despite the hefty price tag, Harding said she has no regrets about her decision. The women bonded over the journey, and in the end, they have a great story to tell, she added.
As for the Bronco, Harding said it’ll be with her for the long haul.
“I slept 12 hours when I got home, and when I woke up, my husband had drove it three times, and he said he wants to keep it,” Harding said. “So, we’re keeping it.”
Tom Costello is an NBC News correspondent based in Washington, D.C.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock valuation looks 'draconian,' even without Jensen Huang: Analyst
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock valuation looks 'draconian,' even without Jensen Huang: Analyst
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia 's stock slid 4.12% Monday in the wake of CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation , leading a broader chipmaker selloff after the chip giant lost hundreds of billions in market cap last week.
The continued decline since Huang's resignation brought Nvidia's stock to its lowest close since July 1, 2025.
Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, after mounting scrutiny following reports that he had a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8.
It was later reported that Huang had romantic relationships with two Nvidia employees. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday.
An online petition calling for Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has drawn more than 170,000 signatures , as prominent tech executives, including Elon Musk , rallied behind him. A source familiar with the matter told CNBC, however, that Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Huang.
Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers are pushing to launch comprehensive investigations into the scandal.
Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and led the company through its meteoric rise to becoming the world's most valuable company, with its AI chips underpinning the technology's boom.
Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia, adding that the board should look outside the company for its next chief executive.
He also suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.
— CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Houthi rebel advance in Yemen may further destabilise global economy
articles.title_zh: Houthi rebel advance in Yemen may further destabilise global economy
articles.content_orig:
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden.
Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world.
Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula.
The country has two coasts: One faces the Indian Ocean on which sits the once-prosperous trading port of Aden, the other faces the Red Sea and, most importantly, the narrow chokepoint at the southern exit of that waterway - the so-called Bab al-Mandab Strait or, in English, The Gate of Tears.
Whoever controls that strait can threaten any or all maritime traffic passing through from both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
In normal times, it accounts for around 12% of global trade, with anywhere between 70 to 150 ships a day making the transit.
But not any more. Although the Houthis say they are no threat to maritime traffic, they are currently at war with Saudi Arabia, making it extremely hazardous for the Saudis to send their oil tankers past the now rebel-controlled coast.
When the US and Israel started a war with Iran in February, Tehran responded by choking off much of the oil trade flowing out of the Gulf through another narrow chokepoint - the Strait of Hormuz. This sent oil prices soaring, boosted inflation and hurt economies everywhere.
The Saudis had a Plan B. Instead of exporting their oil past the dangerous coast of Iran, where their tankers risked being droned or mined by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, they started pumping it overland through their East-West Pipeline to an export terminal on the Red Sea at Yanbu. This worked for a while.
But then in July a cold truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis broke down, that pipeline got hit by drones and the rebels started firing missiles and drones at targets all over Saudi Arabia.
On land, the Houthis seized the initiative and made a lightning dash down the Red Sea coast, sending the Yemeni army into headlong retreat. A brief counter-offensive appears to have failed and the Houthis are now reported to be in full control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the nearby offshore islands.
Nicholas Hopton, a former British Ambassador to both Yemen and Iran and now director-general of the UK-based Middle East Association, says: "The decision by the legitimate government of Yemen to prioritise the military defence of Aden at the expense of withdrawing from other areas suggests that the war is not going well for the Saudi-backed [Yemeni] government. And the rest of the world should be worried."
He warns that if the port of Aden – a city of roughly 1.25 million inhabitants – was to fall to the Houthis, it "would undoubtedly precipitate a further escalation in the regional crisis and further fragility in the global economy, catalysed by the US-Iran war".
But Mohammed al-Basha, the Yemeni founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, believes the Houthis would struggle to capture the heavily fortified city of Aden.
"Any attempt to seize a densely populated city like Aden would come at a significant human cost," Basha said. "Advancing across the flat coastal plains would also expose Houthi forces to air power."
"For now, the Houthis appear to be seeking a negotiated surrender, hoping to exploit infighting and divisions among southern factions to achieve their objectives without a costly urban offensive."
It is conceivable that the Yemen war will settle into a less dramatic but deeply unsatisfactory stasis - a situation where casualty figures subside yet the country remains split between areas controlled by the Houthis - Iran's Shia allies - and the disparate and often poorly motivated forces of the Saudi-backed Yemeni army.
The former British defence attaché to Yemen, Col Iain Smailes, warned that the recent Houthi advance could trigger a spike in oil prices, as it did when they seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait in September.
He also warns this could have a knock-on effect to security well beyond Yemen's borders.
"By extending their control over the western coastline, the Houthis will increase their ability to smuggle weapons and ammunition from Iran, the Horn of Africa and elsewhere, posing additional threats to the region," Col Smailes said.
"This control will enable both Iran and the Houthis to extend their influence in East Africa and beyond."

articles.title_orig: Kalshi plans to launch stock trading soon
articles.title_zh: Kalshi plans to launch stock trading soon
articles.content_orig:
Leading prediction market platform Kalshi will offer stock trading within the next few months, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.
The platform's move to offer equity trading is the boldest so far in its ongoing push into traditional financial markets and comes amid an escalating fight by states and lawmakers against its sports trading business. Sports contracts continue to account for a large share of trading on the platform.
In September, the platform introduced perpetual futures tied to precious metals such as gold and silver after it had originally filed in July to offer beyond prediction market event contracts with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , the federal regulator overseeing derivatives contracts. Perpetual futures are futures-style contracts that have no expiration date.
Kalshi also received approval to list perpetual futures tied to cryptocurrencies in late May.
The prediction market's stock trading offering was enabled by its purchase of broker-dealer FB Securities in July, the source said. FB Securities was founded in Delaware in 2024 and became registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission in December 2025. The broker did not respond to a request for comment.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Kalshi plans to introduce stock trading.
Shares of Robinhood , which offers some prediction markets alongside equity trading, fell on Monday, though the stock was already lower amid a broader market sell-off. Robinhood closed down by 7.8%.
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Army Now Wants Concrete Bunkers For Troops In Israel, Saudi Arabia And Lebanon
articles.title_zh: U.S. Army Now Wants Concrete Bunkers For Troops In Israel, Saudi Arabia And Lebanon
articles.content_orig:
An American soldier has alleged that U.S. military leaders dismissed concerns ahead of an Iranian attack that killed six servicemembers on March 1.
The complaint, submitted Friday to the House and Senate Armed Services committees and first reported by CBS on Sunday, alleges that U.S. Army leaders did not heed warnings about thin fortifications at a command post at Kuwait’s Port Shuaiba.
Iran launched a retaliatory drone attack on the command post a day after the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28. It remains the deadliest attack on American troops since 2021. Over the eight months of the war, a total of 23 U.S. servicemembers have died .
Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, who filed the complaint and was among the dozens wounded in the attack, called the event a “tactical failure” by “the Army, our leadership, and myself.”
Ramsbottom said he had twice raised concerns about the lack of protection from aerial attacks to his superiors but was told, “We don’t have to worry about protection.” He said in an interview with CBS that a counter-drone system “never arrived at Shuaiba and we don’t know if it was ever even ordered to or requested.”
He also alleged that the post had “no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance.”
A day after the attack, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the command post suffered casualties despite its fortifications not because of a lack of preparedness.
“Every once in a while you might have one, unfortunately, we call it a squirter that makes its way through [air defenses]. And in that particular case it happened to hit a tactical operations center that was fortified,” Hegseth said at a press conference. “But these are powerful weapons.”
The Pentagon announced an investigation into the attack on March 3, and the Associated Press reported that it had concluded in June, with a private briefing to families of the slain servicemembers in July. The findings of the investigation have not been publicly disclosed, although widow Michelle Tietjens told CBS that officials acknowledged no mistakes. Ramsbottom’s attorneys separately requested an independent investigation into the attack after filing his Nov. 13 complaint.
TIME has reached out to the Pentagon and U.S. Central Command for comment.
Around a week before the U.S. and Israel launched their attacks on Iran, around 70 members of the U.S. Army’s 103rd Sustainment Command were relocated from Camp Arifjan, a major U.S. base south of Kuwait City, to the smaller outpost at Port of Shuaiba.
Days after the war began, Hegseth told reporters that the Defense Department prioritized protecting U.S. troops and moving “the vast majority … off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire.”
The facility, situated in the civilian port on Kuwait’s southern coast, was within range of Iranian missiles. The Washington Post reported in July that military leaders had ignored intelligence warnings that the post was a probable Iranian target.
CBS reported in March that the post was surrounded by T-walls, steel-reinforced concrete barriers that provide protection from mortars and rockets. Ramsbottom told Colorado news station KOAA in April that the facility was protected from “legacy threats” like mortar fire and car bombs, but not from modern aerial attacks, such as by drones or missiles.
Other survivors of the attack told CBS in April that the unit “was unprepared to provide any defense for itself. It was not a fortified position.” One soldier described the fort as “a bunch of little tin buildings where we can set up makeshift offices.”
The Post reported that a 2021 photograph showed what appeared to be a thin metal rooftop over the building, although it was not clear whether any reinforcement existed underneath.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell rejected reporting that the position was not well-protected. “A Tactical Operations Center is not a ‘makeshift office space.’ The secure facility was fortified with 6-foot walls,” he posted on March 3.
“Every possible measure has been taken to safeguard our troops — at every level,” Parnell wrote.
Multiple news outlets previously reported that no sirens sounded to alert troops before the deadly strike. CBS reported in March that sirens had occasionally gone off after a drone had already entered the base in previous incidents. CBS reported in April that incoming missile alarms had sounded several hours before the attack, alerting around 60 troops to take cover when a ballistic missile flew overhead, and that an all-clear alert had sounded around 30 minutes before the Iranian drone hit. Troops told the outlet that officers had removed their helmets and resumed work at their desks after the all-clear alert.
Soldiers told the Post that the threat warning system was initially not working when a team was sent to scout the post before troops were relocated there. They said repairs had been made to get it operational before the strike happened.
U.S. Army Central previously said in statements to media outlets that the alarm system at the facility was working at the time of the attack.
The whistleblower complaint adds fuel to the fire as Democrats plan to launch congressional investigations into the Trump Administration’s handling of the war when they take control of both chambers of Congress in January.
In September, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Rep. Pat Ryan of New York called for public hearings, citing earlier whistleblower reports about delayed medical care for wounded servicemembers, mistreatment of families, and concerns around the Army’s investigation into the attack. Rep. Maggie Goodlander of New Hampshire described the handling of the attack as “a profound failure of leadership” and said “the Pentagon cannot be allowed to stonewall Congress.”
Democrats and some Republicans have also called for Hegseth to step down or face impeachment , and the latest allegations are likely to intensify scrutiny of his leadership.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D, Conn.), the ranking member on the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, reportedly sent a letter on Sunday to the Pentagon requesting a classified briefing with Hegseth and “all force protection assessments” for the post.
“I’m again demanding full disclosure about the Port Shuaiba attack—an accounting of misjudgments by political appointees likely led to increased vulnerability & greater casualties,” Blumenthal posted on social media on Sunday night.
“The families of the six fallen servicemembers, the wounded survivors, & the American people deserve full transparency & accountability,” he added in another post . “It is time for a reckoning.”

articles.title_zh: Megaspeed says Alice Huang, alleged spy in Nvidia affair scandal, left in 2025
articles.content_orig:
